speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (for the Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: that Bill C-69, an Act to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the third time and passed.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to speak in support of Bill C-69, which implements the policy of spending restraint that we announced in the Budget of February 20.
The measures in this bill have a clear goal: controlling inflation and securing steady non-inflationary economic growth in Canada. I am sure that our friends opposite will support these objectives, especially the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, who is very interested in properly promoting the interests of our country. Attaining this goal will lead to the bright economic future that, of course, we all want for this country.

These measures contained in Bill C-69 are part of the February budget which, through a wide ranging expenditure control plan and with no increase in taxes, reinforces our commitment to address the fiscal challenge. The budget keeps the deficit on a downward track and we will see it cut in half in four years.
Our expenditure control plan takes real action affecting a wide range of federal program spending but it is
also sensitive to the financial circumstances of individual Canadians as well as government. Our plan is helping us to meet the fiscal challenge in a fair and consistent way.
The expenditure restraint measures must be examined as an integral part of the economic strategy we have been following since 1984, and of our response to the current fiscal economic situation. They are part of the government's consistent, comprehensive plan to ensure that Canadians benefit from a standard of living and quality of life that is second to none.
A lot of progress has been made. For example, the burden of government has been significantly reduced. The growth of spending on all government programs and services has been kept well below the growth of the economy and even below the rate of inflation. This is quite a performance.
Our progress toward a better fiscal balance has not been easy. We have all felt the impact of the measures needed to protect and strengthen our future. Many Canadians have had to face difficult adjustments, but the economic pay-off has been considerable.
The success of our economic management plan set out in 1984 is clear. It was the right policy then, and it remains the right policy now. But, as the budget warned, its continued progress is threatened.

Despite our fiscal progress, the burden of the public debt continues to grow, primarily due to the compounding interest on the original debt we inherited. To get off the debt treadmill, we must reduce the burden of high interest rates. To do this, we must deal firmly with high inflation.
The expenditure restraint measures in the February Budget are designed to do just that. I am convinced that our friends oppose, especially the hon. member who is attracting attention as he comes in, will support this policy which is so important for our country. Lower inflation and interest rates and lower deficits will be

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
mutually reinforcing and lead to strong, sustained growth.
Everyone who is able must do their part to help restore the nation's finances to health. That is why our expenditure control plan has an impact on a wide range of government program spending while at the same time remaining sensitive to the financial circumstances of individual Canadians and provincial governments.
I would like to begin by going over two major elements of the plan as it is set out in the legislation.
First, federal program spending. Under the plan, 60 per cent of government program spending is affected to some degree.
To protect modest-income Canadians from the full impact of our expenditure restraint measures, we have exempted major federal transfers to persons, such as old age security, which is not affected, the guaranteed income supplement, which is not affected, spouses' allowances, which are not affected, Madam Speaker, family allowances, which are not affected, veterans' pensions and allowances and unemployment insurance benefits.
So these budgetary measures are extremely sensitive to the needs and interests of people who are less well off. I would like to emphasize one point because I know it is of concern to many individuals: no limit is placed by the expenditure control plan or by this legislation on programs such as old age security, family allowances or veterans' pensions.

The second element I want to touch on concerns transfers to the provinces. Significant deficit reduction cannot be achieved without affecting transfers to the provinces. They are simply too large a part of federal expenses to be ignored. And so this bill includes measures to bring the growth of major transfers to provinces approximately in line with general federal programs spending. This, everybody will agree, is a very reasonable measure to bring the transfers to the provinces in line with our own expenditures.
In 1990-1991 tax and cash transfers to provincial governments will total more than $35 billion. As a whole, transfers to the provinces have risen at an average annual rate of 6.5 per cent since 1984-85. At the same
time, spending on federal programs in general has been held to an average annual growth rate of 3.6 per cent. We believe the provinces as a whole are in a position to bear more of the burden of their own spending. At a time when 35 cents of every federal dollar is used to pay interest costs on the debt, the average figure for the provinces is 12 cents.
As a result of this bill transfers to provinces will grow. I will repeat that. Transfers to the provinces, as a result of this bill, will continue to grow by about 3 per cent annually over the next two years, roughly the same rate as that of total program spending for the federal government.
The reduction to transfers to the provinces represents about 1 per cent of total provincial revenue. At the same time, we recognize the special circumstances of lower-income provinces. Federal support to provinces remains large, total transfers will still increase, and the poorest provinces will receive more growth than others. For example, total entitlements for the major federal-provincial transfer programs are expected to grow an average of about 4 per cent over the next two years for the Atlantic provinces, a growth higher than our own expenditures. While, in the higher-income provinces, they are expected to average 2.3 per cent.
I want to go briefly over the three major programs under which federal support, about $36 billion in 1990-91, is given to the provinces and territories. These are: Established Programs Financing, equalization, and the Canada Assistance Plan.
Under EPF, Established Programs Financing, the federal government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all provinces through the transfer of tax points and cash payments. These transfers were originally designed to help provinces carry out their responsibilities in respect of health care and post-secondary education, but since 1977, provinces have been able to use these transfers according to their own particular priorities.
Established Programs Financing reached $20 billion in 1989-90, an average annual growth rate of more than 6 per cent. The legislation we are discussing today will hold EPF per capita transfers for the next two years to the 1989-90 level. Total transfers will continue to grow with the population increase of each province or about 1 per cent nationally.
June 8, 1990

In addition to EPF, the federal government provides substantial additional assistance to the lower-income provinces through the equalization program. Equalization transfers have grown from over $5 billion in 1984-85 to close to $8 billion in 1989-90. They exceed Established Programs Financing as the largest form of federal support in the Atlantic provinces for example. Equalization transfers to the lower-income provinces are not affected by the budget. They are expected to increase about 6 per cent to 7 per cent annually over the next two years, considerably faster than the expected growth of total federal program spending.
Madam Speaker, I want to make two important points about the effect of this legislation on these transfers.
First, payments will not be cut. Over all, they will continue to increase.
Second, the provinces have complete control of the spending of this money. Whether all or none of it, or any proportion in between, goes to post-secondary education and health care depends on decisions made in provincial capitals, not in Ottawa. It is and remains the responsibility of the provinces themselves.
It is therefore wrong to say this legislation is intended to cut federal support for post-secondary education and health care.
Third, under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government provides funds to provincial and territorial governments to help them pay for social assistance benefits and services. These transfers, which are based on a 50-50 cost-sharing of eligible provincial spending, have grown at an average annual rate of about 6.6 per cent over the past five years.
The federal contribution in the form of cash and transfer of tax points has increased from $4 billion to $5.5 billion. The average rate of growth in each province has varied from 1 per cent to 3 per cent in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Quebec to nearly 14 per cent in Ontario.
For the next two years, growth in CAP transfers will be limited to 5 per cent a year in Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. All provinces receiving federal equalization payments, that is, all provinces whose income is less than
Government Orders
these three, will be exempt from this ceiling on growth. They will continue to have open-ended access to federal dollars to meet any growth in expenditures eligible for cost-sharing under CAP. This measure provides for resumption of the present regime on April 1, 1992.
The 1990 federal Budget, Madam Speaker, will slow the growth of federal transfers in a manner which is sensitive to the situation of low-income provinces-that is very important. The impact on Established Program financing is spread broadly and evenly across all provinces. Low-income provinces will continue to receive large and growing support under equalization. Provinces receiving equalization payments, namely those with lower revenues, will be exempted from the 5 per cent growth limit on cost-sharing under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Despite the enormous difficulties we face in reducing this country's debt and deficit and improving the nation's finances, these are balanced, reasonable decisions geared to the ability to pay of provinces and individuals. We are not like the Liberal government that spent without regard to revenue. We are doing what is right for the country and we want to keep our ability to help people with programs of this kind in future. If we did not act quickly, the Government of Canada would lose its ability to help the most disadvantaged and we will never allow that to happen.
While the provinces are being asked to do their part under the Expenditure Control Plan, as I explained, it is clear that we have restrained our own costs and we will continue to do so. Over the next year, total expenditures on programs other than those that are exempt or capped will decline to a level that is $800 million below that of the current year.

These are real cuts. They reflect the fact that, after several years of restraint, there are no painless ways to cut spending. At the same time, our expenditure control plan balances prudence in managing public finances with the responsibility to protect Canadians who are least able to afford income restraint.
This bill takes a further step along the path we have been following since 1984. It does so with sensitivity toward those in our society who are less well off. It does so in a manner that respects the importance and rights of

the provinces, and that takes account of their economic situations as well as that of the federal government.
I have every confidence that the measures in Bill C-69 are appropriate for our situation and that they are fair and effective.

Madam Speaker, in debating Bill C-69, which the minister has explained in some detail in the past few minutes, I think we are perhaps getting to the very heart of Canadian federalism.
I suppose sometimes the people who watch our debates on television think that they are somewhat strange and maybe irrelevant. Today, more than ever, they hear us debating what sounds, I suppose, rather arcane visions of federal-provincial funding arrangements, when, a couple of blocks down the street, the First Ministers are at this moment discussing the fundamental arrangements among the provinces and the federal government, in fact, the fundamental arrangements among all Canadians whereby we live together in the country.
It would be inappropriate to engage in debate simply on this matter of Established Programs Financing and federal-provincial fiscal arrangements without a word about the more important discussions that are going on down the street, not to debate the merits of the arguments that are being put either way, but merely to say that in a way all that we argue about on Bill C-69 becomes irrelevant if the good will and the wisdom of the First Ministers on behalf of all Canadians do not find a solution to the more fundamental problems that seem to trouble us as a nation.
As we look back into the history of how we fund things like post-secondary education in Canada, we find that there is quite a sense of deja vu. Some of the current debates between the provinces and between the federal government and the provinces sound very much like the ones that occurred in 1864 and have been repeated many times in Canadian history. I think the vast majority of Canadians hope and pray for wisdom and solutions.
These are the fundamentals of our federation. In some ways, the more esoteric topics that we debate as a country about our Constitution are the frills and the extras. The federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, the way we finance the kind of country we want to be, perhaps those are the nuts and bolts. That is the essence of the Canadian federation. How do we fund the country
being and becoming the kind of country that we want it to be? How do Canadians want Canada to develop?
If we could get into a time machine and spin forward into the next century, different scenarios would present themselves; some good, some bad. If you can imagine arriving in the national capital in the year 2020, you might hope, if you could describe the kind of Canada that you want, to discover a country where the people are well educated, where the people interest themselves in examples of the highest of human culture and human awareness. You would hope to find a population that by and large understands the nature of how the world functions, how the economy functions, where the people appreciate the value of literature and art and where the people appreciate the importance that culture brings to the way they live. You would hope to find an economy where we produce high quality value-added products that we sell to the world. You would hope to find a country in which the care for those who are least able to look after themselves is exemplary, where health care is affordable and available to all.
You would hope to not find a country in which the ordinary citizen is not well educated, where illiteracy is rampant, where you find that we no longer debate the harvesting of forests on Vancouver Island because they have all been harvested, where you find that we are still surviving as a nation on the sale of the things that we can dig out of the ground, cut down, grow, or catch in the sea and where we are strictly basing our economy on the sale and production of resources, where we failed to train our people to move forward in competition in a global economy where the need to add value and to make things that the world buys is crucial.
If you look at those two scenarios, Madam Speaker, and say that we definitely want the first one, you might want to go back then and ask what policies should governments in Canada be following in order to ensure that we arrive at that first scenario and that we avoid arriving at the second one.
That in a nutshell for me expresses why the subject matter of this bill is so crucial, so important. I look at it, not strictly as the minister did in his remarks, as a means of getting our financial house in order, although it is that and I understand that, and I will add my words of
June 8, 1990

explanation to the public about why that is the case. However, it goes beyond that.
How we spend money on post-secondary education, on health care and on assistance to the needy in Canada is of crucial importance to the kind of nation we are and are becoming. If this bill does anything, it highlights the critical necessity for Canada, the federal government, and the provincial governments, to overcome the type of debates that are currently going on down the street and to get on with, at least in my opinion, the far more important debate about what kind of country this should be and how do we get there from here. Included in the debate has to be the funding of post-secondary educational institutions, health care and assistance to the needy.
The idea that perhaps we should use these arrangements as a way of trimming back the deficit is something to which the current Minister of Finance seems to have been recently converted. At least back in 1982, when he was in opposition, he did not think that this was really the way to go about cutting back on federal spending. Let me read to you what he said in this House on March 24, 1982 in reference to cuts in Established Programs Financing:
- could have disastrous effects on the universities and on the colleges, on the hospital funding and on the operation of the hospitals. Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems not on the backs of hospitals and universities; let us solve those problems outside of that arena.
I agree entirely with the remarks of the Minister of Finance.
First, let me talk a bit about post-secondary education. When we talk about how important it is for Canada to emerge from this century and go forward into the next one with an economy that moves from our traditional hewers of wood and drawers of water mode into one that highlights the value-added production of new goods, new services, the ability to provide new technologies, and provide information to the world, this requires a broad base of well-educated people. We need a population that is characterized by its commitment to excellence, to its level of literacy and education. It is essential to Canada. This is not merely a provincial matter.
Government Orders
When you go back in history, you discover that this is not a new debate. Back as early as the Confederation debates, 1864, one of the Fathers of Confederation, George Brown, said this about the division of powers:
In thus defining the functions of the general and local governments, it will, no doubt, be objected that we have committed certain matters of an important character to the local bodies which the people of Upper Canada would have been well content to have seen left to the general government. But if the details of the scheme are closely examined, it will be seen that we have given nothing to 1he local bodies which did not necessarily belong to the localities, except education and the rights of property, and the civil law, which we were compelled to leave to the local governments -
That comment by George Brown is very similar to one made in 1864 by Sir Arthur Hamilton Gordon, then Lieutenant-Governor of New Brunswick, who stated:
I ant fully aware of the great difficulties attending the subject of Education, but it is with extreme regret that I see it committed to the Local Legislatures. At all events, the Universities should have been placed under the guardianship of the Central Power. The local governments-
These are his words, not mine.
- needy, rapacious, and ignorant, with little money at theirdisposal, are pretty certain 1o appropriate the University Funds to what they will call more useful objects, that is to say, objects which will enable them to scatter the money among their political adherents.
That is what was said by one of the Fathers of Confederation 126 years ago.
Interestingly enough, as an historic footnote to the constitutional negotiations, the Charlottetown draft of the first constitutional arrangements left the universities under federal jurisdiction. It was only later that that was changed to leave the universities with all education in provincial jurisdiction.
It did not take very long for the federal government to become involved in post-secondary education. As early as 1874, the first military college was established, located at Kingston. In 1885 land was dedicated by the federal government for the University of Manitoba.
In 1910 we had a royal commission on industrial training and vocational education which ultimately gave rise to grants being made by the federal government to the provinces for the purposes of developing agricultural techniques and training and upgrading vocational, technical and industrial education.

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
By 1916 the federal government established the National Research Council in order to assert a federal presence in research in Canada.
This basically continued along until after World War II when the federal government, with the assistance of what became the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, initiated a program whereby universities received $150 grants for each veteran who attended their institutions.
Therefore, the federal government, at the end of World War II, perhaps partly as a means of rewarding those who had gone to fight for Canada, acknowledged the importance of a broadly based, well-educated population. Surely, to a great extent, the success of the Canadian economy through the 1950s and 1960s reflects the fact that we had a higher than would otherwise have been the case influx of well-educated, well-trained people into the workforce, the trained veterans.
In typical Canadian fashion, we have had a whole series of royal commissions, task forces, studies, and special groups study the issue of post-secondary educational funding over the years. We had the Massey Commission in 1951. We had the study of the Bladen Commission sponsored by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. We have had a series of discussions and studies about this issue, most recently in this House. We had the Breau report in 1981. We have had the Senate study it and we have had the Nielsen task force.
What continually comes across when you back through those studies and the discussions and debates that occurred around them is the fact that it was acknowledged by everyone that post-secondary education was too important to the national interest to be only left as a responsibility of the provinces.
For example, on June 15, 1951, Prime Minister St. Laurent said:
Tlie Government has also reached the conclusion that it is in the
national interest to take immediate action to assist the universities to
perform functions which are quite essential to the country.
Partly, this evolved from the fact that universities had expanded their facilities to take care of the increased
enrolment resulting from the veterans who were attending university following the war. In consequence, the expanded facilities had given rise to a greater cost of operation, larger teaching staffs, and so on. In order to maintain the increase in facilities after the veterans had gone through the system, federal participation became essential.
What began then was 16 years of payments of grants to support university education in Canada. Interestingly enough, these grants were made to all provinces except the province of Quebec, which declined to accept any federal participation in post-education within that province. In fact, the funds that would have gone to Quebec were turned over to the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada and held in trust in the interest of the institutions in that province until 1960 when an agreement was entered into between the governments of Quebec and Canada which allowed Quebec to make the grants directly from the provincial government to its institutions within the province.
All of this went through an evolutionary period until about 1966 and 1967 when part two of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act was passed to allow the federal government to make the payments to provincial governments rather than to the institutions in the provinces through the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada.
In leading to this arrangement, we have a statement by the then Prime Minister of Canada, Lester Pearson, about the importance to Canada of post-secondary education. In 1966, he stated:
Education is, under our constitution, a matter of provincial jurisdiction. The federal government does not dispute this or wish in any way to do so. At the same time, education is obviously a matter of profound importance to the economic and social growth of the country as a whole-While education itself is provincial, the federal government accepts primary responsibility for employment and economic activity generally in the country.
He went on to state:
The preparation of our young people for productive participation in the labour force of the country is a matter of vital concern to all Canadians. We have also to keep in mind that young people of a particular province do not necessarily receive their education and training in their home province, and that people, after graduation, do not necessarily live out their lives and take up employment in the province where they received their education.
June 8, 1990

Again, it is a very important acknowledgement of the importance of education to the well-being-economic, social and cultural-of Canada as a whole, of Canada as a nation.
What happened under the 1967 act was that the federal government committed itself to provide to the provinces, for post-secondary education, either $15 per capita of the provincial population, or 50 per cent of eligible post-secondary education expenditures incurred in the province, whichever was higher.
From 1967, for 10 years the federal government was essentially paying half of the cost of post-secondary education in the provinces. There was some revision to that in 1972 when the federal government limited its annual increase under that provision to 15 per cent, and that was pro-rated among the provinces. However, the commitment at that time was clear. Half of the cost of running the university system was federal responsibility.
That created several problems which were overcome with the 1977 arrangement which is really what we are debating today. That program, the 50 per cent support program, tended to distort provincial spending priorities because it encouraged the provinces to spend what were effectively 50-cent dollars. Every time the province spent 50 cents, the federal government, by law, was committed to throw in another 50 cents. Provinces, especially British Columbia, Quebec and, to some extent, Ontario took advantage of those 50-cent dollars in a period of a very broad expansion of the post-secondary education.
The federal government, having undertaken to pay 50 per cent, had no control over the growth of these expenditures. That is a problem clearly for any government; a lack of control.
Third, the federal taxpayer not only had no control, but not necessarily any particular awareness of what the money was going to be spent on. By the time the program was in its last years, more than $10 billion was going from the federal government with no direct control.
The most critical problem with that 50 per cent program was that it required substantial auditing requirements. In other words, in order to ensure that the provinces were receiving the correct amount of money,
Government Orders
the federal government had to investigate what they were spending. This led to all kinds of complications.
Some provinces, for example Ontario, had Grade 13. Other provinces did not. To make it fair, Grade 13 had to qualify for these 50-cent dollars. That meant an argument about how much of the secondary educational system was devoted to Grade 13. Was it pro-rated in some fashion, or how was it worked out? There were even simple problems such as whether Grade 13 students used school buses and, if so, was the federal government not responsible to pay 50 cents of every dollar that was spent on school bus transportation for secondary school students in Grade 13.
Then Quebec introduced the CEGIP system which also was a quasi post-secondary educational institution. Again, there were questions about how much the federal government was obliged to contribute to that.
This led to the Established Programs Financing arrangements of 1977, which is what we are debating the amendments of today. It provided for block funding for, among other things, post-secondary education to the provinces. Those arrangements to the provinces set in course the freedom of the provinces to put the money into whatever they wanted, so much so that, according to a study prepared for the Secretary of State in 1985, some of the provinces were actually spending less on post-secondary education, in terms of the operating costs, than the federal government was giving them.
In 1984-85, according to this study, the provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Manitoba and British Columbia were all spending less on operating their universities and colleges than they were receiving in grants from the federal government. Where the money was going was entirely up to the provincial governments. They could build roads or bridges. They could give it away. They could do whatever they wanted with it and let the post-secondary education system erode.
This itself is not a satisfactory arrangement. For this reason, I must confess to having some sympathy with the problem the federal government has in this area. To some extent, these arrangements have resulted not in nourishing the post-secondary education system, but in allowing the provincial governments an additional source

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
of revenue from the federal government. Meanwhile, across Canada we see many instances of the decline of our universities and colleges.
This latter point is one that we need to be chiefly concerned about. As I said earlier, the health and well-being of the post-secondary education system in Canada is of absolutely crucial importance to our ability as a nation to move forward in the global economy. Surely to goodness, the time has come in Canada-when the First Ministers succeed, as they must down the street in finding a solution to the fundamental problems of the Constitution-for the federal and provincial governments to find an arrangement between themselves to ensure that universities and colleges in Canada are adequately and fully funded.
If we do not do that, it will inevitably lead to a country in which our people are ill-educated and ill-equipped to compete in the 21st century.
All that being said, and recognizing the problems that the federal government has, in my view, it is not enough to go ahead and cut back on EPF right now. I think the Minister of Finance had it right back in 1982 when he said that this is not the appropriate battleground for federal-provincial relations. Many of the things that have been said since the announced cut-backs bring into stark relief the problems that are occurring in our university system in Canada.
In some of our larger universities, the class sizes are enormous. The problems now are totally different from what they were a generation ago. The problems now are technological problems. For example, how do we provide in a lecture hall adequate sound systems and lighting systems so that the vast number of students who have to sit in the lecture hall can see and hear what is being said or taught? We have a need for special lighting systems so that people at the back of enormous lecture theatres can see things that are being written either on over-head projectors or in the odd case on blackboards.
In fact, students in many classes, in many subject areas, are having to go early to their lectures in order to get a seat in the lecture hall.
I am from the generation where we went late, as a matter of religion.
The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada has stated: "It is no secret that overcrowding, meagre library budgets, outdated laboratories, deteriorating physical plants and demoralization of staff and students are all too common on Canadian campuses today. Faced with a funding squeeze, several universities have adopted enrolment restrictions and others are seriously considering such measures".
Since 1977-78, when the current EPF arrangements went into effect, the university system has received a reduction of about 20 per cent in its support per student. Not only are these facts a harbinger of ill things to come in Canada's future if we do not address them because they are of critical importance, but they also directly contradict the kinds of things this government has said.
For example, in August 1989 the Prime Minister stated: "This government will carry its fair share of the burden to ensure that all young Canadians receive a first-class education as they confront a world-class challenge". He is right. Is this the way to go about it, to cut back the one remaining method there is of assisting the provinces in adequately funding education?
The government, I am sure, is going to say that I have not got it quite right, because after all the government does fund research in the universities through the granting councils. Fair enough. The National Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council are very important. I wish I knew how much they were going to be funded next year. The government has not told them what it is going to do about the matching grants policy that expires this year.
On top of that, there are situations where the universities are going broke because of grants from these entities or from problems arising out of the network of Centres of Excellence. Why? Because the granting councils will not participate in funding the overhead for the research. In other words, they will not participate in the costs of laboratories and so on when the research grants are given.
On the one hand, the cut-back in EPF and the failure of the provinces to put what should be put into post-secondary education is stripping the universities of the resources they need to maintain first-class institutions with good equipment and top flight teachers to make
June 8, 1990

sure we have the qualified personnel we need to go into the future.
On the other hand, the money that is coming into research is inadequate to make sure that the universities have the infrastructures and overhead costs covered to carry on the research they are being funded to perform.
We get many examples of what this means. According to an article in the Hamilton Spectator on October 18, 1989:
Tight financial situations and increasing enrolment at universities like McMaster mean faculty are forced to teach more students with fewer resources -
The result is "undergraduate students at McMaster are no longer receiving a decent undergraduate education".
As an example, Dr. Maurer, a psychology professor, said when she came to the university in 1973 she taught a third year-class of 20 students. This year that class has expanded to 170 students.
"Grading 170 10-page essays is like reading War and Peace," she said. "It's clearly impossible."
I suggest that this problem is one that transcends federal-provincial arguments. It is of such critical importance to Canada that we must address it in the context of an over-all review of how we fund post secondary education in Canada.

It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to Members' Statements pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, this week for the nineteenth consecutive year is National Environment Week, from June 3 to June 9. I need hardly recall how much the environmental awareness of Canadians has grown in the past few years.
All governments have a duty to show leadership in this area and promote all environmental initiatives so that, by
the year 2000, Canada will have the best relationship with the environment of all industrialized countries.
In this connection, I would like to draw your attention to an announcement made today by the federal government that $100,000 has been earmarked under the Environmental Partners Program for a major project in the Rouyn-Noranda region. The project consists in placing 28 containers in as many schools to provide for recovery of recyclable waste.
Madam Speaker, this is a concrete example of co-operation between government and the community to provide for better management of our environment and also to ensure that our young people, the elite of tomorrow, acquire good environmental habits.

Madam Speaker, for Environment Week the government produced this beautiful 29-page book on what Canadians can do to help the environment.
One of the useful bits of information it contains is that a single growing tree can absorb up to 21 kilograms of carbon dioxide in a year. A major cause of destruction of trees is, of course, the excessive use of paper.
How well does Environment Canada respect its own admonition to "get involved"?
Of the 29 pages in this book, two are the covers which are on glossy paper, not recyclable; one page contains only two lines of type; there are seven pages which are blank, except for a half-line title, and not one of these pages is printed on the back.
I urge the government to heed its own message, get involved, use paper wisely and save a few trees.

Madam Speaker, I am also pleased to speak this morning about the environment and to join my colleague from the environment committee in bringing to the attention of Canadians the realities of Canadian Environment Week for 1990.

June 8, 1990
I am certainly proud to represent a government which is committed to the environmental imperative as a fundamental principle of its mandate. Indeed, government decision-making has changed dramatically, as environmental considerations gain equal status with economic factors.
Both streams of policy-environment and economics-are critical for resolution before action occurs, if we are ever to truly practise the compelling concept of sustainable development.
The Green Plan consultations which are now being held across the country, constitute a responsible and comprehensive process to bring all Canadians into Canada's environmental movement. Each of us must be a part of this process. It cannot be decreed or imposed upon us, it must be shared. We must all understand the environmental implications of our daily lives.
The Green Plan program arrives in my riding of Fredericton next Monday and Tuesday where citizens will have the opportunity to help build our national environmental consensus. By developing the Green Plan together, we shall ensure its ultimate success which is so essential not just for the sake of our own future but for-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time is up.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on May 31, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Ms. Bourgault) went to Grenville, in her riding, to make an announcement about the Perley Bridge on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board.
She said that Treasury Board had given the Minister of Public Works a mandate to negotiate with Ontario and Quebec representatives with a view to eventually building a new bridge. One wonders whether the Department of Public Works, which has been negotiating this dossier for the last two years, has been doing so illegally, Madam Speaker.
The hon. member also announced, and this made more sense, that funds designated for the requisite environmental assessment would be released following an agreement among the parties concerned. The hon. member also indicated that a three-party meeting was to be held today, June 8, and that the parties agreed that these funds would be released at that time.
The President of the Treasury Board should immediately authorize spending on the environmental study, even if federal-provincial negotiations are still in progress. Otherwise, we may all be faced with a crisis and have to scramble to keep up with events.

Madam Speaker, this week doctors in Alberta joined doctors in Manitoba and Nova Scotia to say that they will stop providing full reproductive health services as soon as their waiting list is exhausted because of the government's new restrictive abortion legislation.
One doctor said: "I don't need the hassles." Another said: "I am being forced into this situation by a crummy law. As an individual I cannot fight the government. We have all tried. It is now out of our hands."
Other doctors, worried about criminal prosecutions and jail sentences, will require signed statements, witnesses and expensive psychiatric evaluations.
The government's unjust abortion legislation not only violates women's basic constitutional rights, it will result in fewer services for women who need them. This unjust law not only reduces Canadian women to second-class citizens in their own country, it tries to make criminals out of women and their doctors.
This unjust law not only violates Canada's U.N. commitments to promote women's equality, it deprives women of full personhood.
This unjust law not only ignores the real issues of unwanted pregnancies, it does nothing to promote family planning, better contraceptive research, and more supportive services for women and their children.
June 8, 1990

Madam Speaker, women are not children. Doctors are not criminals. But this government is guilty of depriving women of their basic rights.

Madam Speaker, there is a place in this very building which they call the red chamber. In the Senate they pay unelected senators $62,000 a year. Last year this amounted to 68 days of work, half the number of days of two years previously.
But $62,000 is not all. There is also $9,800 in expenses, and now an extra $153 a day for every Senator showing up for a meeting.
Canadians should know who their tax dollars are supporting. I think we should have a Senator-of-the-Week contest.
The envelope, please.
This week's senator is Michael Pitfield. He is a former civil servant, with a civil service pension. He is an employee of the huge Power Corporation. He is a Senator. He earns $62,000 a year. And now he gets $153 more.
Mr. Senator, welcome to the trough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe that talking disrespectfully about the other place is not really in order.

Madam Speaker, last week I appealed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration on behalf of Lebanese refugees who are being returned via the United States to war-torn Lebanon.
For the first time Christian and Moslem leaders representing a multitude of denominations have joined together to plead on behalf of the refugees.
I personally know some of these leaders and they are profoundly distressed by the situation of the people in Lebanon. They are calling upon Canadians who have a great reputation for humanitarian values and their government to open their hearts to these victims of war in their country, perpetrated by some of their neighbours.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this past hour the 11 First Ministers began their sixth day of discussion to resolve the impasse on Meech Lake. At no time have these negotiations been more important. Few Canadians would disagree that the future of this great country of ours, as we know it, is at stake. They are watching and waiting anxiously to hear of success.
One such citizen is Tony Pacheco of Sarnia, Ontario. Yesterday he sent me a letter from which I would like to quote:
We are a country built on geographic, cultural, ethnic, and political diversity and adversity. Certainly we are proud of and celebrate our ability to forge a common purpose and still respect and cultivate our differences.
Accommodation, tolerance and compromise are the historical pillars of this country and must continue to be if Canada is to exist.
I am hopeful that in current discussions our First Ministers can embrace these principles. For his part, the Prime Minister continues to demonstrate his commitment and leadership throughout this process.
I, like a majority of Canadians and the members of this House, wish him and the premiers success in today's negotiations of constitutional change.

Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada yesterday decided to risk the health of air passengers and airline employees on the flimsiest of evidence. Although the Non-smokers' Rights Act passed with the support of all three political parties, the Minister of Transport has elected to ignore the will of Parliament and the Canadian people. He has decided to protect Canadian airlines from their own failure to market a unique product, smoke-free international flights, by endangering the health of thousands of Canadians. By delaying the implementation of the smoking ban on overseas flights of more than six hours, the minister is setting back the cause of public health and is discriminating against Canadian workers.

June 8, 1990
Canada has been a world leader in protecting employees and the public from the carcinogenic effects of second-hand smoke. Rather than convince the world of the benefits of breathing clean Canadian air on Canadian airlines, the minister has accepted the airlines' argument that they will lose money, even though no evidence has been produced by them to demonstrate this.
Tobacco is the only legal product that injures and kills when used exactly as directed. I call on the Minister of Nation Health and Welfare to explain the serious health dangers from tobacco smoke to his colleague, the Minister of Transport, so that he will act to protect all Canadians and re-establish Canada as an example to the world of the advantages of butting out.

Madam Speaker, enough is enough. Earlier this week the Liberals who dominate the Senate voted to reward themselves, over and above their generous salaries, by paying themselves $153 every time they show up for work.
Canadians were rightly outraged, as so was I and every member of the Conservative caucus, including the Finance Minister, who correctly labelled the Senate's actions obscene. The so-called rationale that went into that proposal defies logic and is an insult to every hard-working Canadian.
When I read of the senators' plan I thought I had heard it all. Then along came the member for Kamloops who, in an astounding twist of the facts, accused the government yesterday of supporting the senators' proposal-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, I cannot let the member go on. The hon. member for Mount Royal.

Madam Speaker, it seems this government's grab for cash in the deficit battle knows no bounds. It continues regardless of the human and local impact. They have moved now to tax public safety by charging volunteer fire-fighters in municipalities exorbitant 1,000 per cent increases and more for licences to operate emergency radios. In my own riding, the city of Cote St. Luc could face an 1,100 per
cent fee increase because of the government's action. My colleague from Dartmouth has told us of the incredible burden this places on volunteer fire-fighters in his own area.
I warned back in 1986 that the government's Bill C-3 could lead to this but the former communications minister assured Canadians on December 1, 1986, that the changes as they affect municipalities, volunteer fire-fighters and fire departments would not be proceeded with. That has become another hollow promise. We can only hope this budget action does not cause the reduction of emergency fire, ambulance and other services.
Not only has this government imposed the highest income taxes ever, but it now has decided to tax public safety. Canadians are saying, "This has just got to stop. Enough is enough."
* *

Madam Speaker, a recent decision by the Senate, with its Liberal majority, to give senators a tax-free salary increase is incredible.
At a time when the federal government is trying to control public spending and keep a tight rein on inflation, the Canadian Senate has once again demonstrated it does not live in the real world.
It is absolutely incredible to see senators giving themselves $153 per day in compensation, in addition to their salaries, especially when we see how the Senate obstructs the bills of a democratically elected government.
Madam Speaker, I think the government must reject this increase. In fact, I think the Senate deserves a cut in salary or should disappear altogether.

Madam Speaker, the United Nations environment program report, issued this week, once again raises the serious question of child mortality in the developing world. Pollution and other environment-related problems cause the deaths of 14 million children under the age of five each year. In the developing world alone 4.2 million
June 8, 1990

children die annually from respiratory diseases caused by air pollution.
Imagine if you can, Madam Speaker, half the population of Canada dying before Christmas from poisoned air and water, preventable diseases or lack of food. Such a situation would be unacceptable here, and it is unacceptable elsewhere.
We have heard the word "crisis" used a great deal this week. The real crisis is in the developing world where 1.4 billion children live in abject poverty. The time is long past for discussions and debate on the issue of environmental protection. We have the means to inoculate and feed the world's children. What we lack is the political will to do it.
In the minute it has taken to make this statement, 27 more children have died. We must act and act swiftly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, during the last few days, there has been a lot of misinformation spread concerning the Senate's proposed pay increase of $153 per day.
Everyone knows that the government controls the order of business in the other place. One of its cabinet ministers is the House Leader there. Yet, who proposed the pay increase? Was it our former colleague, Senator MacEachen?
No.
Was it the NDP senator, Brother Lawson?
No.
Was it a Liberal senator?
No.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. Oral Question Period.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
This morning, Statistics Canada reported that
43.000	Canadians lost jobs in manufacturing last month. This brings to 120,000 the number of Canadians who have lost manufacturing jobs under the government since January of this year alone.
Why is the government deliberately pursuing a policy of destroying manufacturing jobs in the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government is not following the policy of deliberately destroying jobs. That is a statement that is completely inaccurate.
Five and a half years ago, the hon. member and his party predicted some disaster as far as employment is concerned when the Government of Canada brought out a program for renewal in our economy. The Minister of Finance presented that some five and a half years ago.
In that period of time, we have had unprecedented growth in the economy and in employment. Our record is very good.
At this time, the economy has slowed down somewhat. There is still growth, albeit slow growth. Over the last year, we still created a net 139,000 new jobs. Although the economy has slowed down, we are on our plan to get interest rates and inflation down. Once we get those pressures down, we will see the economy moving again in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this reply is simply incredible. According to Statistics Canada, an agency of this government, in May
43.000	workers lost their jobs in the manufacturing industry. Since January, 120,000 jobs were lost this year.

June 8, 1990
Oral Questions
I want to ask the minister whether this is a deliberate policy on the part of the government, and when the government will change its policy and introduce measures that will create manufacturing jobs instead of destroying them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would never have believed that the Leader of the Opposition would give me the chance to ask Canadians: How can he say what he says?
We want to remove a federal sales tax of 13.5 per cent that totally disturbed the manufacturing sector of the economy of Canada, and he is against the GST.

You are against the Goods and Services Tax. We want to remove the old sales tax to help Canadian manufacturers be more competitive, but no way! Madam Speaker, this party is against any measure that would let the government boost Canada's economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, no wonder the government has no credibility, considering the reply given by the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. It was he and his government who increased the existing tax four times since they came to power, a tax which according to him is harming our economy, and now they want to introduce a GST that will increase inflation in this country!

Yesterday, Robert Blair, chairman of Nova Corporation, said at the meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association that the government's "crude and cumbersome" economic policy "has driven up the value of the Canadian dollar, hammered our exporters, and is endangering the nation's standard of living".
Will the minister admit that his policies are endangering the country's standard of living, and that the people who have to bear the brunt of his government's mismanagement are the 120,000 Canadians who have lost good manufacturing jobs since January?
Why does the minister and his government continue with these policies when he knows they are creating massive job losses and are expected to cause the loss of thousands more at plants such as Kelsey-Hayes in Windsor over the coming months?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to go back to what the Leader of the Opposition said about the manufacturing reality of Canada.
He knows very well that, at the present time, the international economy is going toward globalization. Because a lot of Canadian industries have to rationalize their operations, we face a lot of operation on that level. As a Canadian and as a minister of the government, I would hope that the member agrees that one of the ways that we have to help the manufacturing sector is through decreasing the federal sales tax.
The hon. member does not agree with that. He does not agree that we can totally remove the manufacturers' sales tax to put in a goods and services tax, which will be applied not only to Canadian manufacturers. I do not understand him, but I know what the economy that they had in 1980-84 gave to Canadians.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and concerns the constitutional impasse. Negotiations are entering their sixth day. The atmosphere is pretty negative, and Canadians are very worried about the course of events. I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether he could give the House a progress report on the negotiations and let us know whether, should the impasse continue, the plan is to continue the negotiations over the weekend.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the discussions of the First Ministers have reached a critical stage.

June 8, 1990

As the hon. member is aware, I am sure, the talks did reconvene this morning. I am satisfied that there is still a strong will to reach a satisfactory conclusion by all First Ministers and others who are involved in the process.
We can only hope that their deliberations this morning will result in further progress toward reaching a satisfactory conclusion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question, Madam Speaker.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister assure us that the Prime Minister will give a full accounting of the situation to the House of Commons today, or whenever the negotiations are terminated, even if it means calling back the House of Commons during the weekend?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that has always been the Prime Minister's intention.
On previous occasions when these discussions took place, at the first opportunity, he sought to come before the House and to report in full detail. I have no reason to believe that that would not be the case on this occasion.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology as well.
As the minister responsible for the manufacturing sector in the country, does he not have a sense that in fact there is systematic destruction of our manufacturing base taking place right across the country? Since November, 1988 when the Conservatives were elected again,
183,000	manufacturing jobs have been eliminated. The minister can suggest all sorts of red herrings such as the manufacturers' sales tax.
Is he not prepared to admit clearly that his ministry has not taken action to protect the jobs of Canadians in the manufacturing sector and has not been able to take action against the present government's policies which are so detrimental to the manufacturing sector in Canada?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is entirely inaccurate in what he is saying.
For example, there was just a major announcement in his own community of Windsor where Chrysler is investing some $400 million in two or three plants to upgrade and bring up to standard, which will preserve and increase employment for people in his own constituency. He knows that. For him to stand up and make a statement in the House as he did is totally wrong.
The other problem in the manufacturing sector right now is that the wage demands being asked now are inflationary. We are seeing it, and the Minister of Finance has said it many times. They are forcing Canadians to be uncompetitive.
I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that labour costs grew 8.2 per cent last year, while productivity increased only 1.7 per cent. That is why we are uncompetitive. Wage demands must get more in line with productivity if we are going to compete. That is the message that is out there. It is inflationary to have an 8.2 per cent increase in labour costs. It causes the problems we are experiencing at the present time.

I have a supplementary question, Madam Speaker. I would just say that the minister should get real.
According to the latest Economist, the rate of growth of industrial production in the country is the worst among the G-7 countries for last year. We are not succeeding.
The minister has mentioned my community. Let me ask a question with respect to my community. Yesterday, over 1,500 people from Windsor, from right across the community, protested against the shutdown of Kelsey-Hayes. It was a shutdown of a company which made $8 million last year and yet has shifted three of its production lines to Missouri.
Will the government use the two million shares it owns in Kelsey-Hayes and Varity Corporation to see that these jobs are protected and saved for the future of our community?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I agree with the hon. member who knows very well that Varity had a covenant in that it had to protect, maintain, or create jobs in its

June 8, 1990
Oral Questions
companies. I expect that the company will live up to its commitment.
The question is not that jobs have to be protected specifically at Kelsey. Jobs have to be protected by Varity within the plants belonging to Varity. The hon. member knows that very well. The covenant will be respected.
I believe that, as far as the headquarters is concerned, the 1986 agreement determined that the number of jobs will be protected and that will be done, However, the company does not have to give the guarantee that it will be done at Kelsey, specifically.

Madam Speaker, the point is that this company has an important government shareholding in it. In the past, the minister responsible for small business said that the shareholding would be used to help protect jobs in this company. It has not been.
Is the minister not prepared to listen to those 1,500 people who in the streets of Windsor yesterday said: "Our jobs are being hit and our families are being hurt"? Is he not prepared to listen? Is he not prepared to act for the sake of our country? Do something.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope the member from Windsor does not want to give the House the impression that we are not sensitive to people who lose their jobs. We are as sensitive as the hon. member. We do not have the magical answers that the hon. member seems to have.
I never said that we would not be open to listening to those people.
My friend knows very well that a great many steel wheels are being replaced with aluminum wheels. This is something that creates problems in that type of industry. We are sensitive to that. We are working with the company.
We are very sensitive to what happened to the workers. It would be more sensitive to look to having an industry which could continue to be competitive with industries across the world.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
When Manfred Ruhland and his partners were given Route Canada they paid $29 million, none of which was their own money. Then the government turned around and asked CN to give Route Canada $40 million so that it could lay off 1,500 workers. What a deal!
How can the government possibly say that it made a good deal when it gave away $11 million more than it got in return for a $100-million corporation?

Madam Speaker, there are a lot of allegations and a lot of figures in the hon. member's question. Let us put everything in perspective.
The purchasers of Route Canada paid $29 million for a company with an asset base of $40 million or $50 million. The company was losing $40 million to $50 million a year. That is not much of a return on investment in any business, in any country. That is what happened.
In the efforts, CN, the company which sold the asset base, felt that selling it as a going concern would give those employees a better opportunity to see if they could make a go of it. Unfortunately, they did not make a go of it. Everybody regrets that. Nobody takes any pleasure in people losing jobs. But that is part of the competitive system that we all believe in.
CN came to the assistance of some employees who wanted to take their pensions, and they did so. I do not think CN should be chastised for that either.

Madam Speaker, Route Canada which was given $40 million and which got rid of 1,500 employees still could not make a go of it.
During the election campaign the government was afraid that Route Canada truckers were going to disrupt the election campaign, so it got CN to carry out negotiations with them. When the election campaign ended so did the negotiations.
Why did the government lead Route Canada workers to believe that negotiations were being carried out in
June 8, 1990

good faith when all the government wanted to do was to shut them up until the election campaign was over?

Madam Speaker, I think what we have to decide here is whether we take into account the unfounded allegation of my friend or a letter written on CN's letterhead to The Toronto Star in an effort to put in writing the facts as they are, not on an unfounded allegation.
In that letter it is stated: "In the process we negotiated special agreements to help ease the impact on employees not required to operate the new company profitably. We have met every one of our commitments to employees, pensioners, customers and communities, including the payment of $23 million for separation and related costs of former CN Route employees".
I ask the House and everybody watching to compare that with the unfounded allegation of my friend.

Madam Speaker, I would like to follow up on the question that I asked in the House yesterday. It is with respect to the sworn statement of Manfred Ruhland, who stated that he had dealings in this transaction with the then Minister of Transport, Donald Mazankowski.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House if he had any dealings with Manfred Ruhland before the sale of CN Route, during the negotiating process or after CN Route was sold to Manfred Ruhland?

I believe, Madam Speaker, that my friend has inadvertently misread what the actual question in the alleged-heavy on the "alleged"-affidavit of the individual concerned is. I do not think he did it intentionally.
It states: "Who represented CN in the negotiations and sale of TRC?" That is not as put by my hon. friend.
If he is going to read all the names, I would hope he will pay attention to the word "maybe" in the sixth line.
Madam Speaker, I have read the document fairly thoroughly-

Fairly!
Oral Questions

I appreciate the comments of my friend with respect to that transaction. I might say that I am very pleased to hear the answer that I suspect I heard, that is, that there were no dealings. That just goes to show that this company was sold to a person, a most undesirable person, who took this company and destroyed the lives of 1,900 people.
Since we cannot always deal with legal obligations between parties, does the government not now have the moral obligation because of this transaction to look after the affairs and the pension benefits that rightly belong to those people who devoted so many years of their lives to CN Rail?

Madam Speaker, I want to start off by thanking my friend for withdrawing the allegation of yesterday. I think it is important to this whole affair that that be done. I appreciate that.
I think we should look at the letter in total. It lays out the facts of what kind of money was being lost. I have read a previous statement to the House so I shan't read the same statement. There is another statement that is very important. It is: "Our alternative to the sale was to close down CN Route and lay off all staff in 1985". To lay off all staff and close down was the alternative.
The letter continues: "We chose to sell to purchasers who agreed to use their best efforts to continue in business as a national common carrier. As a result, this is what happened".
"CN and no one else decided to sell its subsidiary after discussions with more than 30 companies beginning in 1985".
This letter is on CN letterhead, and I will table it. It continues: "Our negotiations on the sale were held directly with David Fingold representing himself and his brother Paul as principal purchasers. Their financial credentials were very solid".

Madam Speaker, three times in the recent past my leader and I have raised questions in this House with both the

June 8, 1990
Oral Questions
Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare about what the government plans to do to ensure that GST rebates to those on welfare will not be deducted by the provinces.
Three times we have received vague and sanctimonious answers. My provincial colleagues have been asking the same questions of ministers in their provinces.
My question is more specific. It is directed to the Minister of State for Finance.
Has the deputy minister been instructed to clarify this concern with the provincial governments at the upcoming Deputy Finance Ministers' Conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will have to take that question as notice and discuss it with the Minister of Finance. We will get an answer for the member.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to get yet another succinct reply.
I would then like to ask this question of whoever over there answers these questions. Will they give an undertaking that they will attempt to get from the provincial counterparts to the Minister of Finance an assurance in writing that the millions of Canadian on assistance will not have their GST rebates clawed back and that the matter will not be left in the laps of the gods, who in this case are the provincial finance ministers?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance has expressed his concern many, many times about the behaviour of provincial governments when benefits are provided by the federal government. There are certain jurisdictions in this country that give provinces and the federal government certain powers. We are all becoming very much more aware of that in the discussions that are proceeding at the present time.
The Minister of Finance has been very vocal in his concern that the benefits that flow from the federal government to beneficiaries in this country of ours are received by them and are not taxed back by the provincial government. He will continue to make those representations in the strongest possible manner.

Madam Speaker, can the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology give us the name of one Canadian manufacturer who has phoned him up and said: "Keep up the good work. You are doing a great job, Minister. Your high interest rate, high dollar policies are just what we need to compete"?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Even in French, Madam Speaker-excuse me, obviously it would take me far too long to give the hon. member all the facts although he must be familiar with the situation that prevailed before 1984. I believe the government's record for industrial development has been excellent. The results are there. I repeat, we are now in a phase where Canadian companies must adjust to international competition and, as a result, are restructuring their operations and must also deal with anti-inflation policies. We are coping. However, I am inclined to think the hon. member was being funny when he asked his question.

Madam Speaker, this government's industrial policy is not funny. It involves cuts to R and D and cuts to employment and training. It involves a high interest rate, high dollar policy that is driving Canadian manufacturing jobs south of the border, just so that they can compete under free trade.
What is the result? The result is that since free trade we have lost 172,000 key manufacturing jobs.
Is it a deliberate policy of the government to drive Canadian jobs south of the border? When will it realize that its economic policies are destroying our future? When will it wake up and stand up for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing that we should hear such comments in the House of Commons. Even the Premier of Ontario is promoting a free trade agreement in the United States and all across the world.


June 8, 1990

The Royal Bank said: "Trade deal fuelling investment jobs". "Free trade helping Canadian business" was another statement made. We have a lot of examples.
The premises are wrong. We want to put money into employment. The bill is being stalled in the Senate. It is a bill for money and for jobs.
The Liberals are not serious. They never had a policy. We have sound industrial and economic policies.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister or the Government House Leader.
As the minister knows, the Senate, in order to break the impasse with the House of Commons has introduced a-
They voted themselves an increase. That will help the impasse. Your Liberal friends now have an incentive to come and sit down and do their jobs.
They are looking for more days of work so that they can get the $153.

Madam Speaker, as I said, the Senate, in order to break the impasse with the House of Commons, has introduced a motion to refer Bill C-21 on unemployment insurance to a conference between the two Houses, which is the established way of dealing with such differences between the two Houses.
They have a self-interest now. We are paying them to sit down.

As a matter of fact, there have been 10 such conferences since Confederation.
I want to ask the minister responsible if the government is now ready to respond to the Senate and participate in such a conference to resolve the differences between the two Houses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, you can tell from the reaction to that question that we on this side are tremendous admirers of that other place.
Oral Questions
We think they have been acting very responsibly, particularly recently.
The Senate has sent back its amendments to Bill C-21 which, incidentally, would have added $2 billion to the deficit. This House rejected those amendments and sent them back.
The Senate has sent back a message insisting on those amendments, something that is questionable, certainly from a propriety point of view, since it is this House that establishes the fiscal policy of the country and not that House.
