Madam Speaker, before Question Period, I was giving a few examples of the problems we find in our post-secondary education system here in Canada, and I mentioned some problems at McMaster University in Hamilton.

There are problems though throughout Canada in post-secondary education. They are a signal to us that we are at risk in Canada of imperilling our economic well-being in the future because of the failure of our system to produce trained and well educated people.
I will take you Madam Speaker, on a brief tour across Canada.
In the University of Manitoba Department of Computer Science, for example, courses for non-specialists in computer science have had their class sizes increased to over 200 people and line-ups to use computer equipment are commonplace because there is not enough equipment to go around. One computer course for non-specialists was eliminated altogether due to lack of funds. Three faculty members in that program have resigned-one to go to the United States, one to teach in high school and one to join the private sector. In all three cases, it was in order to obtain pay increases.
Another professor says that in his classes he has embarked on trying to shake down the class size, since they are so large, through a process of intimidation and refusing the students the right to ask questions so as to encourage them to drop his course.
In Newfoundland at Memorial University, Dr. Leslie Harris, the president, has recently had to announce an interim hiring freeze. He says that further measures are going to be taken to make up the difference in the short-fall in the university budget. Dr. Harris stated:
We have eliminated approximately $4 million from capital operating costs and many of the projects we have had to drop are of critical importance. These include such things as roof repairs, road improvements, classroom renovation, replacement of desks and other classroom equipment, repairs to tunnels and other necessary projects.
Dr. Harris said that inadequate funding is reflected in the ability of the administration to provide services and facilities for students. He said:

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
The fabric of the place suffers. Old plant and equipment which breaks down, the deteriorating quality of classrooms and classroom materials, desks, audio visual equipment, the lack of space for recreation and social activities-these are some of the prices we pay when we cut back.
With regard to the University of Alberta in Edmonton, a newspaper report in The Leader-Post of Regina in April of this year stated:
The University of Alberta has adopted a plan to freeze enrolment at its current level next year.
The board of governors voted in a closed meeting last week to limit enrolment for 1990-91 to the present level of 29,500 students. This means entrance requirements could be raised to a 73 per cent average mark from 70 per cent.
The problem is also reflected in the level of tuition fees in the universities. The Canadian Federation of Students has made this point and has raised the prospect that many qualified Canadian students are unable to pursue their education because of the sky-rocketing tuition fees and other costs.
For example, between 1989 and 1990-91, tuition fees have climbed at Memorial University in Newfoundland from $1,280 to $1,344; Dalhousie University, from $1,710 to $1,771; and Mount Allison in New Brunswick, from $1,935 to $2,135. Quebec is exemplary in respect of tuition fees, but even it has had a significant increase. McGill University went from $570 to $890. At McMaster in Ontario it went from $1,516 to $1,637. I could go on across the country, province by province.
If I might be permitted, I will comment on the relevant weight of tuition fees.

The Province of Quebec has set an example for the rest of Canada in the way it handles tuition fees for students. If we want our students to be well educated and well prepared for the future, we must reduce, not increase tuition fees.
Quebec has set that example; tuition fees are as little as one-third or one-quarter of what they are in other provinces. Surely, if we put a high value on education we would see to it that cost does not prevent people from pursuing their education.
Going on, George Pedersen, President of the University of Western Ontario, issued this stem warning:
The university system in Canada is in trouble. Serious trouble.
Mr. Pedersen said that the quality of instruction available to university students today is not nearly so good as that provided to their parents who attended an Ontario university 30 years ago. Class sizes are now much larger, laboratory equipment is outdated, students get more of their instruction from graduate students and part-time instructors instead of regular professors. Mr. Pederson further stated:
The reinstatement of quality in our universities is, without question,

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-69, the Government Expenditures Restraint Act.

This 5 per cent will cover inflation and, consequently in real terms, the financial assistance provided to the richer provinces in Canada by the federal government for the social welfare system will experience no growth whatsoever.

Those people who will be affected are the sick, because these are expenditures which have been reduced to the health care system, students and those working in our post-secondary education institutions because of cuts to post-secondary education. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-69. It is an important debate about a bill that raises serious concerns right across this country.
The formal title of this bill is "Government Expenditures Restraint Act". There is a saying, "What is in a name?" When it comes to this particular bill, there is a lot to this name and all of it is very bad.

Let us consider the seriousness of the situation from this perspective. Let us take the time period between the fiscal year 1986-87 and fiscal year 1994-95. The cuts in that period amount to an astronomical $31 billion. If these cuts had not occurred under the government, there would have been $22.2 billion more for health care in the provinces, and $8.9 billion more for secondary education.
Let us look at the effects of this and other Tory initiatives on health care. If current government practice continues, the federal government will soon cease paying a single cent for health and education by the turn of the century. That is alarming. There will be no more federal

Despite all that, that wretched system which does not deliver to its people, costs more per capita than does Canada's universal system. Yet there are these powerful forces in Canada, whose only battle cry is fiscal restraint, who would move our health care system closer to that of the U.S. model.
I say to the government: "Wake up, open your eyes, and smell the coffee or smell the flowers-whatever is appropriate. Freezing federal payments to the provinces is a virtual invitation to destroy medicare."
The government's backing away from payments to the provinces and medicare is consistent with what this administration has been doing since it was first elected in 1984.
The 1980s were really a lousy decade, in some ways reminiscent of the Dirty Thirties. What started as a disturbing trend at the beginning of the 1980s was greatly exacerbated by Tory policies.
I would like to make reference to a newspaper column which was written May 16 last by Frances Russell of the Winnipeg Free Press, one of Canada's leading commentators on public affairs. In her column, she makes use of facts and figures provided by the Canadian Council on Social Development, and she quotes comments made by one David Ross, an independent social economics consultant based here in the nation's capital. I want to quote
Government Orders
from that column because it paints an absolutely superb picture of what has been going on in Canada in the last few years and it points the finger where it ought to be pointed-right at the Mulroney government.
The decade ended with 155,000 more Canadians unemployed than at the beginning. There were 62,000 more poor children. There was a virtual standstill in household income. Whereas average family earnings rose 27 per cent in the 1950s, 53 per cent in the 1960s and 42 per cent in the 1970s, in the 1980s they went up a meagre nine per cent, largely due to a decline in family size.
The rich got richer and the poor got poorer. The share of national income enjoyed by the lowest 29 per cent of Canadian families shrank from 10.7 per cent to 10.4 per cent. By contrast, the wealthiest 20 per cent of Canadians saw their portion rise from 42.1 per cent to 43.2 per cent.
That means, Ross says, that during the 1980s, about $4.2 billion was transferred from the poor to the rich.
Ross says the starkest images of the 1980s poverty were the homeless bedding down in shelters and the hungry queuing up at food banks. "Not since the breadlines of the 1930s has Canada witnessed such a shameful reminder of the shortcomings of the labour market and the holes in the income safety net."
Government policies were intent on heightening social and economic inequality.
"The decade was marked by the status quo or retrenchment in existing social programs. More decision-making was transferred to the marketplace. Thus began the era of trickle-down, an economic philosophy that wealth should be generated at the top simply by removing economic shackles (mainly taxes) with ensuing gains eventually trickling down to middle and lower income workers".
Ross attributes the phenomenon of homelessness and food banks to the tightening of unemployment insurance, which threw more people faster onto social assistance, and to the failure to maintain social assistance rates even at the poverty line.
No social policy area was harder hit in the 1980s than family benefits, he says. As a result of partial de-indexing, they lose 3 per cent of their value each year. Already, the worth of family allowances has shrunk 12 per cent since 1980.
The new clawback of family allowances and old age security from "rich" Canadians will work down the income scale at 3 per cent a year (again due to partial indexing) until middle and finally, lower income Canadians will be shut out.
Ross contrasts this contraction of public pension benefits with the piling on of tax breaks or private pensions, also out of the public purse-The federal government's 1985 tax reform was a further giant step back to inequality. The tax changes between 1984 and 1990 meant, for a one-earner family of four, an increase of 21 per cent at the $20,000 level, 28 percent at the $50,000 level, 3 per cent at $80,000, but a saving of 1 per cent at $100,000.
Ross is not optimistic that the 1990s will bring immediate change.

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
"The liberalism of the 1970s, characterized by strong government involvement and high levels of public spending, was replaced in the 1980s by a conservative trend. The decade will be remembered for government cutbacks, privatization, concern with the deficit and market decision-making-"
That is the end of that particular series of quotes and that column says it all. It really does, it says it all.
I would submit that those who are watching the Parliamentary Channel right now, whether in Newfoundland, British Columbia, or my home province of Manitoba, will understand why we Liberals are dead set against Bill C-69. It contains just more of what we have come to expect from this government: VIA Rail services cut; postal services cut; farm support programs cut; unemployment insurance cut; native programs cut; federal transfer payments-it all depends how you express it-either frozen or cut, but either way inimical to the best interest of the provinces, inimical to the best interest of Canadians, inimical to the best interest of the health care system, and inimical to the best interest of post-secondary education in the country.
Sad to say, it is the same old story from a government that does not believe in government, that does not believe in governing. This government has completely, absolutely, without reservation, abdicated its responsibilities. I think it is time to put this government away and put it away for a long time. May it never be seen again. If it does not want to govern, if it does not want to take its responsibilities seriously, I know a group of people on this side of the House who are more than happy to take on that responsibility, more than happy to govern the country in the best interest of all Canadians and not just a privileged few. It is palpable that it is not only us who are saying this. Canadians are saying it by the millions through the polls.
Bill C-69 is a very bad bill. The government is going to regret this legislation. It will regret this legislation and the Canadian people will make absolutely sure of that.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague for a very fine speech, a speech that accurately and adequately represented the comments that we are hearing from Canadians right across the country, and certainly that I am hearing from people in my own riding of Nepean.
He talked about reduced transfer payments to the provinces for education and health, in particular. He talked about the goods and services tax, the imposition of this tax upon Canadians and how it is going to hurt them. In addition, he talked about how the cuts in transfer payments and how the GST are going to hurt the provinces. The speaker talked about the clawback, how it is going to hurt the senior residents and about the cut-backs to the native programs.
These are only a few of the cut-backs that we see in this bill. The one thing that comes to my mind when I read of the dreadful measures in Bill C-69, is that Canada, as we have known it for 123 years, is being changed. How the programs have been administered all these years also comes to mind.
In my opinion, with the federal government giving more responsibilities to the provinces, I see a serious abdication of what we have considered to be and what we have known as the federal responsibility in this country for 123 years. It is decentralizing the federal powers and putting them on the backs of the provinces. Then the provinces, in order to maintain the level of the programs that we have known, obviously will have to increase taxes at that level. I would like to have the hon. member's comments in regard to an abdication of responsibilities on behalf of the federal government.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Nepean. I think her beginning words were far too generous.
Let me pick up on what she said. There has been an abdication of federal government responsibility, especially the responsibility toward the provinces. My understanding of Canadian history, and, particularly, Canadian government history, is that there has been what one might call a family compact of provinces. At the centre of the compact is the federal government, the central government, that has a strong responsibility to all the provinces, especially to the poorer provinces.
The provinces cannot be left to fend for themselves. The provinces cannot be left to drift. The federal government has a responsibility to all the provinces, to the entire country, so that we, regardless of where we live, enjoy a certain basic standard of living. That is not
June 8, 1990

going to happen under these cuts to or freezing of federal transfer payments.
As sure as God made little green apples, this is going to hurt the poorer provinces. Eventually it may even hurt rich provinces like Ontario or British Columbia, but it will hit the smaller provinces like Manitoba and Newfoundland especially hard.
What we are facing is the balkanization of Canada. In the current constitutional proposals, we see an allowance for provinces to opt out of a national scheme, and at the same time get federal money. I find that provision enormously alarming. That is going to work against the best interests of the smaller, poorer provinces.
Perhaps a rich province like Ontario can make it on its own, but the smaller provinces cannot. This calls for a strong central government that cares about all the provinces and has policies that bind the country together to make it whole. One makes the country whole in many ways. We have heard this expression very often through the Meech Lake discussions.
There is a lot of truth to it, but one does not make a country whole through only some constitutional niceties or constitutional rules. One makes it whole through social programs and federal transfer payments, which constitute very important social programs. If the federal government, at the very centre of a program diminishes it, it diminishes the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are this afternoon on this late spring day discussing whether or not the government should cut $8.3 billion in assistance to the provinces. My colleagues and I say no. We say the government has no moral authority, has no possible excuse or reason why it should want to cut $8.3 billion in program money to be transferred to the provinces. That is exactly what the government wants to do with Bill C-69.
On February 20, 1990 this House heard the second budget from the Minister of Finance since the November 1988 election. Contrary to the previous year's budget, this budget was all released on the same day, rather than over a series of days as was done the previous year.
Government Orders
All members were sitting in this House listening attentively to the Minister of Finance. We thought we would hear words of wisdom from him. We thought we would hear a thoughtful speech on how this federal government wanted to work together with the provinces in order to provide a decent quality of assistance, not just to the provinces, but, to Canadians generally who utilize the services which are offered by the provinces. That is really the most important thing of all.
Instead, my colleagues and I were shocked to hear the following, and I quote from the minister's speech:
We have capped the growth of a number of programs at 5 per cent per year for the next two years. These include Canada Assistance Plan payments to the fiscally stronger provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta; and certain expenditures for science and technology, and Indian and Inuit programs. In the 1989 budget, defence and foreign aid expenditures were substantially reduced. In view of the tight fiscal situation, their growth will also be limited to 5 per cent from this lower expenditure base.
If that was not bad enough, he then said further:
We have held a number of programs at their 1989-90 levels for the next two years. Total per capita cash and transfers to the provinces under Established Programs Financing will be held constant.
This is newspeak, "will be held constant". That means the same as "will be frozen" but the newspeak expert across the way, the Minister of Finance who brought us other similar weasel words, this time told us that the financing will be held constant which of course, as I said previously, is a euphemism for a freeze.
This is what he announced and Canadians listened to him. At first, I suppose, one could be almost tempted to believe that these cuts were necessary. I say almost tempted, because of course no one truly believes any more what the government across the way says. In the unlikely event that some might have been tempted to slightly believe some of what the Minister of Finance said, we came to a rude awakening once we started to make the calculation and determined that provinces would have to cut back on services that they offer to Canadians, or increase their own provincial income tax or in turn, if the provinces could do neither, they would have to transfer some of those same expenditures by reducing their own transfers to municipalities.

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, this expenditure restraint program, as I said earlier, announces the government's intention to freeze federal transfers to the provinces under Established Programs Financing for the next two years and, during the same period, to cap federal transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan to Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta at 5 per cent.
I would like to expand on this particular point, Madam Speaker. There are those who will say that since Ontario is richer than the other provinces, these cuts will have practically no impact. Well, that is not true. Anyone who thought that was the case is badly mistaken.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg St. James (Mr. Harvard), pointed out earlier and very eloquently, I may add, that of course the poorer provinces would be hit more severely and would possibly feel the impact even more quickly than other provinces.
Madam Speaker, although some people may think everybody in Ontario is rich, that is not the case.

I have made a comparison of electoral districts in the province of Ontario. The Minister of Finance represents the riding of Etobicoke Centre and perhaps he feels that all of Ontario is the same as his own riding. That, of course, is not so.
I have made a comparison of the riding of Etobicoke Centre and the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, which I represent. The information I am quoting is from a document entitled, Profiles: Federal Electoral Districts-1987 Representation Order: Part 2, a publication of Statistics Canada. These are quite valid, genuine Statistics Canada figures in case someone would think that I was partisan and perhaps would use statistics other than official ones.
This is what these statistics show about these electoral ridings. First of all, Etobicoke Centre has 89,160 people living in it; Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, as of the 1986 census that is, had 87,140 people. As you see, Madam Speaker, both ridings are just about the same in terms of total population.
Let us look at some statistics which indicate the general socio-economic condition of the riding that I represent and demonstrate to this House that it is not the same as the riding of the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding the fact that it is also in Ontario.
If we look at the following statistic, total population with level of schooling less than grade nine, 6,960 in the riding of Etobicoke Centre and 13,845 in Glengarry- Prescott-Russell. It is the same size in population but has twice as many people who do not have a grade nine education.
The number of people with a university degree in Etobicoke Centre is 13,255; in Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, 3,780, with the same size population, notice the difference.
Let me read the following statistic to you: total labour force 15 years of age and over, 52,000 in Etobicoke Centre, and 42,000 in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
As you see, Madam Speaker, not all of Ontario is the same, and perhaps the Minister of Finance should look elsewhere rather than just his own constituency when trying to determine what he thinks is good for all of us.
Let me read a few more statistics: managerial, administrative and related occupations-let us see how many have big-boss jobs in Etobicoke Centre versus Glengarry-Prescott-Russell; in Etobicoke Centre, 6,155; in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, 2,780.
Continuing with the statistics: females in the workforce, 23,825 in Etobicoke Centre, 16,760 in Glengarry- Prescott-Russell.
The total number of occupied, private dwellings is given as 32,000 in the riding of Etobicoke Centre and
28,000	in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. That is nearly the same, Madam Speaker.
Now let us look at the average value of a home, which is usually a fair indication of the socio-economic standing of the people: $176,149 in Etobicoke Centre and $77,036 in the riding that I represent.
The statistics show government transfer payments offered to various electoral districts and in Etobicoke Centre, 5.7 per cent of the revenue comes from government transfers. In my own riding it is 11 per cent. This clearly indicates that any cut made by the minister has an

June 8, 1990

effect which is twice as bad in the riding that I represent than elsewhere.
I am trying to indicate that my riding needs assistance. It needs the help of this government, and it deserves the help of this government.
It has a right.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
It sure does have a right, as my colleague from Nepean said very eloquently. However, when it comes to getting what is rightfully yours, this government of course does not deliver.
I want to read about income characteristics. The average income for males with income 15 years of age and over in Etobicoke Centre, $35,916; in Glengarry- Prescott-Russell, $22,127; average income for a female in Etobicoke Centre, $17,428; in Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, $12,243.
If cuts are justified any place in Ontario, surely my colleagues in this House will agree that the riding I represent cannot afford to share in any part of the cut-backs imposed by the government across the way.
Finally, I would like to read one last statistic which will indicate beyond doubt the difference in economic situations: average family income for all census families in Etobicoke Centre, $60,725; Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, $36,771.
What we need in the area I represent is not cut-backs. What we need is not the cold, callous way of doing things which this government has shown it can do so well. What we need are programs to assist the region I represent, enabling it to gain a higher standard of living similar to that enjoyed by people elsewhere.
The riding I represent is not located thousands of miles from Parliament Hill. It may be surprising to some to know that the statistics I have just read apply only 40 miles from Parliament Hill. That is the distance to the heart of Prescott County from where we stand right now.
Under the previous Liberal administration there were a number of programs which had succeeded in attracting industries to our area and improving the living conditions. These have all been abolished by the government across the way.
Government Orders
The government through these cuts will affect grants to the provinces, and if the province has to cut back, which area can afford it the least? The one that I represent and others like it.
It is all very well in the government's eye to talk about cut-backs, but I say to them that if any area is equipped to absorb them it is surely not the one I represent.
[Translation\
Madam Speaker, we must not think for one minute, just because Ontario happens to be very well off compared to other provinces, that this applies to every single person in the province of Ontario, because it certainly doesn't apply to Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. The riding I represent will certainly have trouble surviving and coping with the cutbacks the Minister of Finance gives us in his Budget and in Bill C-69.
The government sees Tory members applauding and supporting the initiatives proposed by the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister probably imagine the applause of Tory back-benchers reflects the feelings of Canadians in general. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker, and it is certainly not the case among the people I have the honour and the privilege to represent in this House.
What we need, Madam Speaker, is a government with heart, a government that will be mindful of the needs of Canadians on low and modest incomes, and as I pointed out earlier, there are a lot of people in my riding who belong to this group.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance to swallow his pride for a few minutes, and I even challenge him to rise in the House now, Madam Speaker, and withdraw Bill C-69. We on this side of the House, my colleagues and myself, would be delighted to give the unanimous consent that is necessary to withdraw a bill from the House of Commons. This bill will cause a lot of suffering both in provinces that are less well off and in the so-called rich provinces.
This bill certainly does not contribute to national unity because we know as long as such great regional disparities exist, they create tensions.

June 8, 1990
Government Orders
Furthermore, this bill certainly does not help my constituents.
I therefore appeal once again to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of Transport, who is known for his generosity, Madam Speaker, and ask them to withdraw this bill. We know that the transport minister is generous. The Department of Transport showed its generosity in the past when they gave a Crown corporation worth nearly $100 million to one Manfred Ruhland. We already know how generous the finance minister is. Some people, or rather a very small group of two or three rich people, benefited from his generosity in the past.
What we want, Madam Speaker, is to be sure that low-and middle-income citizens can also benefit from the generosity of the government opposite.

In closing, I ask the Minister of Transport to pretend for a minute that my constituent's names are all Manfred Ruhland, that every single one of them is called Manfred Ruhland, and let us have the Minister of Transport treat my constituents with that kind of generosity. I am not asking the Minister of Transport to give airline passes to my constituents to fly all over the world or anything like that. I am just asking him not to impose those unfair cut-backs that he is proposing to us today.
The Minister of Transport may be speaking for the Minister of Finance today, although I think the Minister of Finance who is here among us is quite able to defend himself. In any event, for some reason the Minister of Transport wants to defend the Minister of Finance. I would hope that he would stand now and withdraw this bill which is unfair, not only to less financially-able provinces, but indeed has a severe impact on all Canadians, on their health care and on their level of education. Most of all, it has a negative effect on what we are all trying to do, which is to ensure that all our citizens are able to improve themselves and participate on an equal basis in the society of tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the presentation made by the member. I thought it was very effective, especially in the way he compared the constituencies in Ontario, and demonstrated that there are some low-income people who are going to be suffering as a result of the cuts in
transfer payments and the capping of the CAP in Ontario.
I want to talk about Manfred Ruhland. The hon. member suggested that he hoped all his constituents would receive the same treatment as Manfred Ruhland did. Unfortunately, if all his constituents were Manfred Ruhland, he would probably be representing a Tory riding. The guy who could not get a credit card most likely had a PC card.
I would like to talk about another constituency in Canada. It is a constituency all across Canada. It will be taking the hardest impact of the EPF cuts. Low-income Canadians will be taking 46 per cent of all the cuts in this budget. These are people who are living at the poverty level in Canada. There are millions of them across the country. They are single parent families headed by women, most of whom are found below the poverty level.
As you know, Madam Speaker, poverty goes hand in hand with illiteracy. The same people who tend to be poor also have difficulty with literacy skills. They will end up having difficulty as a result of the cut-backs in EPF funding. In fact, it has been pointed out that something like 6.8 million Canadians between the ages of 16 and 69 are unable to accomplish everyday tasks such as reading newspapers, making out cheques, reading bank statements and, generally speaking, functioning as normal Canadians.
These people lack the kind of literacy skills that are needed in order to function on a day-to-day basis in the modern world. All the government is giving to these people is something like $110 million over five years. Madam Speaker, you will know that in the national capital we spend $105 million a year watering lawns in the area.
Certainly, it shows what kind of priorities we attach to poverty and illiteracy in the country. We are supposed to be joining with countries internationally to conquer illiteracy. We spend five times as much watering the lawns in the national capital area as we are going to be spending on literacy this year. At the same time, we are cutting back on programs that help to support health care, the elimination of poverty and post-secondary education in the provinces across Canada.
June 8, 1990

I think it is tragic that the Conservative government holds those kinds of priorities. I appreciate the statements that the hon. member has just made on the priorities of this Tory government.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

Madam Speaker, I want to take a moment and indicate to my colleague who has just spoken the fact that single parent families are a phenomenon of all our constituencies.
In the riding that I represent, there are 2,000 such families. Perhaps that number is slightly lower than the number in other electoral districts, but I invite my colleagues to compare it with the fact that the average female in my riding who is working earns $12,243 a year, something like one third of what the average female in the constituency of the Minister of Finance would earn. It has a very devastating effect.
In closing, I do indicate that, in terms of the comparison, the literacy problem is a very serious one. I do not dispute that, but I am not one who would advocate that we stop maintaining the public property around the national capital. speechtext: It being 2 p.m., the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed in today's Order Paper.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FINANCE FEDERAL TRANSFER PAYMENTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FINANCE FEDERAL TRANSFER PAYMENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of ensuring that federal transfer payments to provinces for the purposes of education and health care are spent directly on those services.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to discuss the question of accountability of provincial governments for funding provided to them by the federal
Private Members' Business
government under the Established Programs Financing system for the support of health care and post-secondary education.
If I may just read my motion, I am suggesting:
-the government should consider the advisability of ensuring that federal transfer payments to provinces for the purposes of education and health care are spent directly on these services.
Essentially, this motion calls upon the government to explore making federal transfer payments to the provinces accountable for the purposes for which they are transferred. Particularly in the context of transfers under the Established Programs Financing legislation, the motion calls for ways to make sure that that part which has been traditionally transferred to the provinces to fund post-secondary education and health care is used for those purposes and not for other purposes.
As is well known, the federal government became involved in financing post-secondary education, at least by 1912, when grants were made in support of agricultural education. The involvement gradually increased from these modest beginnings with the temporary program of support for veterans returning to Canada after the Second World War.
In 1951, the federal government introduced a matching scheme of direct grants to universities. Starting at 50 cents per capita per annum, the grants rose to $5 per capita per annum by 1966.
With the 1960 Technical and Vocational Training Act, the federal government laid the foundation for the establishment of community colleges through federal-provincial agreements. The federal government paid 75 per cent of provincial expenditures for community colleges.
In 1964, the federal government became involved in student assistance when, in conjunction with the provinces, it launched the Canada Student Loans Program.
In 1967, a fiscal arrangement was entered into by the federal and provincial governments whereby federal government direct grants to universities were replaced by a shared-cost arrangement with the provinces. Under this agreement the federal government paid 50 per cent of the costs of post-secondary education institutions. At the same time, the shared-cost program for technical colleges, begun in 1960, was replaced by the direct purchase of student places at community colleges.

June 8, 1990
Private Members' Business
In 1977, the federal government withdrew from shared-cost financing and replaced it with unconditional fiscal transfers under the EPF arrangements, the arrangements which we are now living under. As is well known, these transfers were in the form of cash and the transfer of tax room to the provinces.
During this development of funding support for postsecondary education the federal government, of course, also instituted its participation in funding research in Canada and, perhaps more important, its participation in funding health care in Canada.
I set this out not just as a walk down memory lane, but to make it clear that the federal government has long been involved in funding post-secondary education and health care in Canada.
Even though the EPF legislation introduced in 1977 provided for unconditional transfers to the provinces, both the federal government and the provincial government have been fully aware of the history and the intention for these funds to go toward health care and post-secondary education.
When present ministers were in Opposition they pointed out the importance and the fact that these funds were designated or intended for health care and post-secondary education, although they do appear to take a different point of view now.
There was no intention for such payments to be for highways or for other expenditures over which the federal government had little interest. The federal government's funding of post-secondary education and health care stems from a national interest to ensuring a high quality education system in Canada to which all Canadians have equal access, and to ensuring a high quality and accessible health care system in Canada.
The national interest in both post-secondary education and health care clearly persists today, as statements made by the Prime Ministers and others in the present government have indicated.
Much has been made of the fact that some provincial governments have been spending some of the money transferred from the federal government under the EPF program for other than post-secondary education and health care. In earlier times this was used to argue for a return to some accountability on the part of the provinces for the money transferred from the federal government. This argument at least recognized the importance of two things-federal financing, because of the national interest in high quality, accessible post-secondary education and health care on the one hand and, on the other hand, making sure that federal money designated for post-secondary education and health care was in fact used for these critically important purposes.
However, and to disastrous effect, the present Conservative government has used the problem of provincial governments using EPF funds for other than post-secondary education and health as an excuse for cutting back on the funding, thus accentuating the very serious financial problems faced by Canada's post-secondary education institutions and by our health care system. This irresponsible and short-sighted action by the Conservative government is in sharp contrast to its rhetoric about the importance of both post-secondary education and health care in Canada. It has led to a critical situation.
With regard to education, for example, Dr. George Pederson, President of the University of Western Ontario and current President of the Association of Universities and Colleges in Canada, has publicly stated that the state of Canada's universities is a national disgrace and places Canada in serious jeopardy of being unable to train Canadians to meet the demands of the country's economy in an increasingly competitive world. Without immediate and drastic corrective action, this can only lead to Canada's deterioration to Third World economic status.
Canada's post-secondary education systems and health care systems are suffering from a sharp decrease in federal government funding, inadequate provincial government financial support and misspending of federal funds intended for post-secondary education and health care to other purposes. All this has led to a critical deterioration in the ability of Canada's post-secondary education system, for example, to offer the type and quality of post-secondary education which is required today in Canada, and has led to the situation in which our health care system is unable to cope effectively with the health care needs of Canadian citizens. This is illustrated by the fact that many Canadians in British Columbia and Ontario, at least, are having to go to the United States for certain health care procedures, and
June 8, 1990

that we have had long waiting lists at hospitals for surgery. Indeed, we have had examples of Canadians dying because of being turned away from our hospitals.
Again with regard to post-secondary education, the federal government in spite of the hope generated by the Saskatoon forum has shown no leadership whatsoever in attempting to ensure that Canada's post-secondary education system is world class, as it needs to be. In fact the federal government has instead attacked the system through major cut-backs in funding support.
The federal government has been roundly criticized by all actors in both the post-secondary education system and the health care system in Canada for its disastrous policies and lack of leadership for which future generations will pay dearly. Instead of complaining that provinces do not always spend Established Programs Financing funds on post-secondary education or health care, the federal government should take steps today to ensure that the provinces spend these dollars as required, that is, on post-secondary education and health care. It is in the national interest to do so. It is irresponsible, short-sighted, indeed, foolish and dangerous not to do so.
It would be prudent for the federal government to ensure that EPF funds intended for post-secondary education and health care are spent by the provinces on those two things.
The current pleas of the federal government are to reduce the deficit and to ensure that federal revenues are spent wisely. Surely, such arguments should also go for EPF transfers and should ensure that those transfers are indeed used for health care and post-secondary education.
Both the post-secondary education institutions in Canada and our health care system are in severe need of adequate funds to do their job adequately, as far as education institutions are concerned, to prepare Canadians for the 21st century and to ensure Canada a viable future; and as far as the health care system is concerned, to ensure that Canadians are able to lead a happy, healthy and dignified life.
Ensuring provincial accountability is a critical component of resolving the funding crunch experienced by our universities and colleges and by our health care systems.
Private Members' Business
Many have called for greater accountability on the part of the provinces.
For example, a 1980 parliamentary task force called for a tight accounting of how provinces used federal transfers. The Johnson report argued for the federal government tying its increases in federal funds to increases in provincial expenditures. Indeed, the Nielsen task force argued that there should be a different approach to the use of EPF funds and, indeed, that they should be more accountable in the hands of the provincial governments.
I will just quote briefly from the Nielsen task force. It states, in part: "We note that provincial governments would object to any new option"-that is to say a new procedure for ensuring that they spent the moneys on post-secondary education and health, as required-"because no other arrangement could likely offer them the combination of revenues and unconditionality with respect to post-secondary education that the present EPF arrangement provides. Nevertheless, in the view of the study team, it is of the greatest importance that the government develop a new direction in consultation with the provinces".
I am not alone in calling upon greater accountability. As we all know, prior to 1977 there was total accountability on the part of the provinces with their funding for post-secondary education and health care in their use of federal transfers.
If the federal government was truly committed to high-quality, accessible health care and high quality, accessible post-secondary education in Canada, then it would ensure that its financial transfers to the provinces are increased to meet the needs of universities and colleges in Canada and the needs of Canadians. It would not drastically cut funds, as it has done. It would also ensure that the moneys transferred to the provinces under EPF are in fact used for post-secondary education and health care.
It should begin discussions immediately with the provinces to ensure the accountability of federal transfers. It should use the influence it has, stemming from its spending powers, to make sure that post-secondary education and health care funds are used for those purposes.
There is no excuse for not acting on this right away. Indeed, not doing so and not transferring adequate funds

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to the motion before the House.
The motion suggests that the government should ensure that federal transfers for health and education are spent directly on those services. There are a number of reasons for rejecting this motion.
Let me reiterate that supporting such a motion would be contrary to the spirit of the Established Programs Financing arrangement which the federal and provincial governments agreed to in 1977 when they moved from cost sharing to block funding for health and educational services.
Under EPF the federal government provides a contribution to provinces in respect of both health and post-secondary education. Provinces can allocate these funds according to their own priorities which may vary greatly in different parts of the country.
Requiring the provinces to provide a detailed accounting of every dollar they spend on post-secondary education and health care, as the motion suggests, would be a tiresome and unjustified administrative burden for both the provinces and the federal government. We would prefer the money went to the provision of services to Canadians, not to do unnecessary accounting.
Re-imposing conditions on the provinces with respect to how they spend EPF money would also be legally contentious. For example, at present there is no accepted definition of what constitutes post-secondary education. Attempting to arrive at a legal definition would no doubt launch the federal government into a lengthy and expensive legal wrangle.
Above all, re-imposing what would have to be detailed conditions on the provinces would reduce their flexibility in providing innovative health and education services. This would, in a very real way, inhibit the development of Canada's world-class health care system, and it would smother creativity in Canada's first-class post-secondary education system.
Canadians are proud of their health care and education systems. They are a good measure of the wealth and the compassion of our society.
Education, in particular, is increasingly important to making our way in the competitive world in the 1990s and beyond. Canada must have an education system that is responsive to change, that can adapt to help Canada meet the challenges of international competition. Education and human resource development and training will determine which countries are in the vanguard of economic development and which are in the rearguard of economic decline.
Canada already spends ample amounts on education, second only in per capita terms to Sweden among the industrialized countries. What is more important here is not money. It is value for money-it is results. We must not put policies in place that threaten to constrain innovative approaches to post-secondary education. This is obviously even more important in the field of health care where human lives are at stake.
The federal government has been and remains committed to quality education and health care in every region of Canada. While education and health generally are assigned to provincial jurisdictions under the Constitution, there has always been a federal role in these areas. Federal involvement in supporting post-secondary education can be traced back to its role of providing direct support to veterans and to universities in the post-war period. Joint health programs began with the national health grants which were part of the post-war reconstruction program.
With the development of a nation-wide health insurance system, and the rapid expansion of Canadian post-secondary education facilities in the 1950s and 1960s, the federal government's role in financing both health and post-secondary education increased dramatically.
Under cost-sharing arrangements, the federal government contributed about 50 per cent nationally of what were defined as the eligible costs of hospital insurance, medical care, and post-secondary education institutions. The cost-sharing approach was taken at a time when both health and post-secondary education programs were in a stage of major development and expansion, and when the Canadian economy was growing rapidly and governments could afford to devote large sums for these purposes.
June 8, 1990

By the mid-1970s, it had become quite clear to both the federal and provincial governments that the costsharing approach was no longer viable. The open-ended nature of cost-sharing arrangements reduced the federal government's ability to control and predict its expenditures. Wide per capita variations in federal transfers to different provinces appeared inequitable. Cost sharing of specific expenditures led to rigidities and an inefficient allocation of resources. The arrangements were cumbersome to administer because of auditing requirements and difficulties in defining eligible expenditures. The approach encouraged expenditures at both levels of government through 50-cent dollars.
In an effort to overcome these problems, the federal and provincial governments accepted in 1977 that cost sharing would be replaced in favour of Established Programs Financing.
Let me briefly review the objectives of this financial arrangement. They are to maintain across Canada the standard of services to the public under these major programs, and to facilitate their improvement; to put the programs on a more stable footing so that both levels of government are better able to plan their expenditures; to give the provinces flexibility in the use of their own funds which they have been spending in these fields; to bring about greater equity and equality among the provinces with regard to the amount of federal funds they receive under the program; and to provide for continuing joint policy discussions relating to the health and post-secondary education fields.
Under EPF, the federal government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all provinces through the transfer of tax points and cash payments. The federal government continues to pay a substantial share of the costs of provincial health and post-secondary education programs. In 1990-91 federal EPF contributions will amount to over $20 billion.
Let me reiterate, Madam Speaker, that since 1977 the provinces have been able to use these transfers according to their particular priorities rather than in the more restricted fashion required by the previous cost-sharing arrangements. This system works well. It has given Canada a health care system that is the envy of the world. It has provided us with world-class universities and post-secondary institutions.
Private Members' Business
I would ask hon. members to bear these facts in mind when considering the motion before the House.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this motion that is before us brings the whole question of federal payments to the provinces and, in particular, payments under the Established Programs Financing Act. It is a very important subject.
In 1977, we saw a major change in the way in which federal assistance was delivered to the provinces. The federal and provincial governments agreed back then to replace the old shared-cost program and shared-cost method of assistance with a very different kind of program which we now know as EPF.
Through the EPF program the federal government continues to support the financing of a number of programs, including, of course, post-secondary education and health care. Provincial programs are supported through payments made directly to their governments.
The change in 1977 was to move away from the old shared-cost system, where federal assistance met up to about half the cost of certain programs, to a system of what is called block funding.
Federal assistance is now based on a formula related to the growth of the economy and of the population of each province and is therefore more equitable across the country. The provinces are happy with this arrangement. I am certainly not aware of any objections since 1977 to that arrangement, since it allows the provinces more flexibility in designing programs to use their revenues, both those raised by themselves and those provided by the federal government.
Over the years there have been changes in the EPF program, but all have respected the basic principles of that act and the agreement between the provinces and the federal government.
Most recently, the federal government has responded to our financial situation by proposing changes which ask the provinces to share in the national burden of fighting the deficit and inflation. These changes, too, respect the outlines of the EPF program.
June 8, 1990

I want to take time now to look at these recent changes in light of our situation with respect to this motion.
At this point, it is important to remember that total federal transfers to the provinces through tax points and cash payments amount to over $35 billion. These transfers have grown at an average rate of 6.5 per cent per year since 1984-85-a rather significant growth rate. This compares to spending on federal programs which has grown in the same period by an average rate of 3.6 per cent per year. That is certainly less than the rate of inflation, but substantially less than the rate at which we have been transferring payments to the provinces.
We believe that the provinces are able to carry a larger share of the burden of their own spending, especially the more prosperous provinces.
At the present time, 35 cents of every federal revenue dollar is being used to pay interest on the accumulated federal debt, while the comparable figure for the provinces together is only 12 cents.
I have talked about more prosperous provinces sharing the burden that we at the federal level have. I would like to talk specifically about the province that I live in, the province of Ontario. I heard the doom and gloom about funding for various health care and education programs because of this cut that we have proposed in EPF. I say cut, but it really is not a cut. We are increasing transfers to the province of Ontario by over 2 per cent, almost 3 per cent.
Having said that, in all the doom and gloom that members of the Opposition have talked about, the province of Ontario this year was able to increase its spending on health care by 12.8 per cent in its budget. Where in the world is the doom and gloom that members of the Opposition are talking about?
Not only was the Government of Ontario able to increase its spending by 12.8 per cent in the field of health care, it was able to balance its budget. It was able to pay off some of its debt. All in all, it was doing a pretty remarkable job. I give it credit for that. The fact is that the province was able to raise the money. Yet here we are in the House saying that the province of Ontario could not afford to get only just under 3 per cent more from the federal government. That is nonsense.
Private Members' Business
Our expenditure control plan will limit the rate of growth of these transfers to about 3 per cent for the next two years. This is about the rate we ourselves are holding to for federal program spending. In other words, all we are asking the provinces to do is to carry the same load that we here in Ottawa are putting upon ourselves. We are asking them to do as we are doing-not more, not less.
Having said this about the provinces in general, however, we are sensitive to the fact that some provinces are not in as good a position as others. I understand that, yes, the province of Ontario was able to do some things because of some economic health that it has. As a result of our planning, our plan is sensitive to the needs of individual provinces. Federal transfers will grow by about 4 per cent a year in the next two years to those seven weaker provinces, while the stronger ones, including the province that I come from, will only grow at just over 2 per cent a year.
However, I want to underline another important aspect of our proposal. It is that the reductions we are proposing are really not reductions. They are reductions in the rate of growth, but they only amount to about 1 per cent of the provincial revenues. It is not 10 per cent, 20 per cent or 40 per cent. I realize opposition members have not used those numbers, but the hysteria they create by the way they are carrying on suggests that we are decimating provincial revenues. That is nonsense. It is about 1 per cent.
Transfers will, of course, continue to grow. The weaker provinces will benefit more than the stronger provinces. That is part of what Canada is about.
I want to look more closely now at one particular area of federal transfers, the Established Programs Financing, which is the focus of the motion that is before us today.
EPF is the single largest element of over-all federal transfers to the provinces which amount to about $36 billion in 1990-91. EPF itself has grown from $14.5 billion in 1984-85 to about $20 billion in 1989-90. That is a growth rate of over 6 per cent a year.
We at the federal level have been controlling our spending at a rate of 3.5 per cent a year. We have been transferring money to the provinces at the rate of about 6 per cent a year. They certainly have not been very hard

Since 1977, however, the provinces have been able to use the money in accordance with their own priorities. They have not been dictated to by the federal government. Each and every province can set their own priorities in using the money that we have been transferring to them.
Of course, in 1977, I need not remind you, Madam Speaker, and unfortunately for Canada, there was not a Conservative government in Ottawa. An awful lot of bad things have happened since 1977 because of another government that existed in Ottawa, but in this particular case on that point that government transferred responsibility to the provinces. That, in essence, is what Canada believes in, that the provinces have the responsibility to deliver. We give them that responsibility.
Our proposals will continue to transfer under the EPF for the next two years at the same per capita rate as they got in 1989-90. It is not a new formula. It is the formula they used in last year's budget that we are asking them to use it in this year's budget and in the next year's budget.
Transfers will therefore continue to increase as provincial populations increase at an expected rate for the country as a whole of about 1 per cent. Because transfers are based on an equal per capita figure for each Canadian, the effect of our program will be equal for each and every province.
In 1992-93, the rate of growth will return to that set out in the law and in the agreements which provide for the payments to increase by the rate of inflation less than 3 per cent, as announced in the April, 1989 budget. After 1992-93, the rate of increase will not be less than the rate of inflation.
The second program under which the federal government assists the provinces is the equalization program, which provides help to provinces with weaker revenues and which may be directed to health care and post-secondary education. These payments have also grown strongly in recent years, from about $5 billion in 1984-85 to nearly $8 billion in 1989-90, a 60 per cent growth rate in about five years.
In the case of the Atlantic provinces, these payments are more important than payments under the EPF simply because of the sheer size and volume of the payments. Equalization going to the less prosperous provinces is not affected by the restraint program presented by the government. They will continue to grow at a rate between 6 per cent and 7 per cent a year, which is substantially higher than the projected rate of increase in federal program spending.

While we are asking the provinces to share the burden, as I have explained previously, we are continuing to spend a great deal of money, up to $27 billion in 1990-1991, on the two programs in actual cash. That is a substantial proportion of federal government spending and an even higher proportion of spending of federal programs.
These moneys are being transferred to the provinces because we believe the provinces, which have the constitutional authority in the areas of education and health care, are the level of government best suited to make the practical decisions about what services are to be delivered and how they are to be delivered. Without an increase in the size of the federal bureaucracy, this is the most efficient and effective way to ensure that Canadians receive the services they need.

speechtext:
Before I begin, Madam Speaker, let me congratulate my colleague for his excellent speech. I think he conveyed his position with great maturity.
In 1977, there was a very important change in the way federal aid was given to the provinces. The federal and provincial governments agreed to replace the shared-cost assistance with a considerably different funding mechanism, now known as Established Programs Financing. Under EPF, the federal government continued to fund a large part of provincial post-secondary education and health care programs by transfer payments to the provincial governments. The difference is that starting in
June 8, 1990

1977, the federal government would no longer contribute on a 50-50 shared-cost basis with the provinces. The federal contribution would be calculated on the basis of the economic growth and population of each province. The federal government's contribution to these programs thus became more uniform across the country. The provinces were satisfied with this arrangement because it gave them much greater flexibility in using funds both from their treasury and from the federal government.
Much has happened since then and our assistance continues in spite of straitened circumstances. In the current fiscal year, transfers of tax points and cash to the provinces will total over $35 billion. On the whole, transfers to the provinces have increased at an average annual rate of 6.5 per cent since 1984-85. By comparison, spending on federal programs in general has been held to an average annual growth rate of 3.6 per cent, which is less than the rate of inflation. In general, the provinces are able to carry a bigger share of their spending, especially the provinces that are in good financial shape.
At a time when 35 cents of every dollar of federal revenue is used to pay interest costs on the debt, the average figure for the provinces is only 12 cents.
Under the Expenditure Control Plan which was part of the last budget, the tranfers to the provinces are expected to grow over the next two years by nearly 3 per cent a year, roughly the same rate as the federal government's total program spending. In other words, we are not asking the provinces to carry a burden heavier than our own. We are asking the provinces to do their part, that is all.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I should like to emphasize the federal government's contribution to the provinces, a contribution which remains very significant. The transfers generally will continue to increase and the less affluent provinces will benefit from a higher growth rate than the others. Because the transfer payments to the provinces represent very significant amounts, I should like, if I may, to deal a little more in detail with the way the governement helps all provinces.
In 1990-91, the federal government will provide nearly $36 billion in total financial support to the provinces and territories.
The greater part of this assistance comes under three major programs: Established Programs Financing,
Private Members' Business
equalization payments and the Canada Assistance Plan. Under the Established Programs Financing, the Federal Government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all provinces through the transfer of tax points and cash payments. These transfers were originally designed to help provinces carry out their responsibilities in respect of health care and post-secondary education.
Since 1977, provinces have been able to use these transfers according to their particular priorities. EPF transfers are the largest single form of federal support to provinces, and have grown from $14.5 billion in 1984-85 to about $20 billion in 1989-90, an average annual growth rate of more than 6 per cent.
In addition to Established Programs Financing, the federal government also provides substantial additional assistance to the lower income provinces to help them provide public services including health care and postsecondary education through the equalization program. Equalization transfers have grown strongly in recent years, from over $5 billion in 1984-85 to close to $8 billion in 1989-90. For example, they now exceed EPF as the largest form of federal support in the Atlantic provinces.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan (CAP), Madam Speaker, the federal government provides funds to provincial and territorial governments to help them pay for social assistance benefits and services. These transfers, which are based on 50/50 cost-sharing of eligible provincial spending, have grown at an average annual rate of about 6.7 per cent over the past five years. The federal contribution, in the form of cash and transfer of tax points, has increased from $4 billion to $5.5 billion. The average rate of growth in each province has varied from 1 to 3 per cent in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Quebec, to about 14 per cent in Ontario.
For the next two years, growth in transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan, or CAP, will be limited to five per cent a year in the fiscally stronger provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Other provinces-those receiving federal equalization payments- will be exempt from this ceiling on growth. They will continue to have open-ended access to federal dollars to meet any growth in expenditures eligible for cost-sharing under CAP. Implementation of this measure will provide for resumption of the present regime on April 1, 1992.

June 8, 1990
Private Members' Business
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that federal financial assistance to the provinces is distributed on a progressive basis. Fiscally weak provinces receive far more substantial per capita assistance than the richer provinces. The facts show, beyond a doubt, that the federal government has done its share despite a financial context, a financial situation of which everyone is well aware, and I am referring to our very substantial national debt and deficit. I believe that in times like these, we must be realistic. We must be realistic because everyone wants more assistance. Everyone wants better programs. Everyone wants an even more progressive increase in programs. However, we must consider the country's financial situation, and I believe that Canadians are very well informed in this respect and are very proud of the fact that we are able to act responsibly as a government.
As my colleague from Halton-Peel (Mr. Turner) said, we were not elected to this House or to government just to win beauty or popularity contests. We were elected to show leadership and the ability to run this country well.
I think that for this reason, Canadians will be grateful to us for having done the right thing at the right time, Madam Speaker, for having made the right decisions when they had to be made and for not trying only to win popularity contests in the short run.
Madam Speaker, thank you for your attention. [English]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FINANCE FEDERAL TRANSFER PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to rise on this Private Members' Motion dealing with federal-provincial relations. I speak from some 11 years of sitting in this House and listening to the same debate over and over again. One hundred years from today members will still be debating this because the bottom line reality is that we live in a federal country with a federal power that has enormous taxing power against all Canadians in all regions of the country. It deals with provinces which represent much smaller areas, often with much less strength to be able to tax their people and industries.
Since Confederation mechanisms have been developed to transfer cash through the central Parliament back to regions that do not have the same taxing authority.
I can remember soon after 1980 sitting on a federal task force of all three parties in the House looking at the question of federal-provincial transfers. We travelled to every provincial capital and interviewed dozens of Canadians, provincial governments and officials. It became crystal clear that there is one thing that the provinces are absolutely unanimous on, and that is that if they can help it, they are not going to give up any fiscal power to the federal government and that they want more and more fiscal power back.
Indeed, the genius of Canada is that in times of crisis, war and depressions, for example, power can centralize in Ottawa as happened in World War I, World War II and during the Depression. However, during peace time there has been a steady devolution of fiscal responsibility to the provinces.
To me the most important thing for this Parliament is to ensure that we never give to the provinces that residual power that we have, i.e., peace, order and good government, so that at a time of crisis, whether an economic crisis or a political crisis such as war, power can be taken and used by Parliament.
In the meantime, during peace times, very likely the principle that the government closest to the people gives the best government is a good principle to operate by, and so we should not be frightened by that.
In terms of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, we know from the speeches given earlier that the federal government, using its spending power, moved into areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. That is the real critical point. We are talking about that limited area where there is exclusive provincial jurisdiction- property civil rights and education. Property and civil rights includes hospitals.
We should not easily move into those areas and try to take them away from the provinces. Indeed, if we did, the Supreme Court would throw it out and declare any act of Parliament to be unconstitutional. So we have had to enter into arrangements.
The first one was shared cost under which the provinces would get 50 cents for every 50 cents they spent. Under that, the provinces, particularly the ones that had strong fiscal capacity, built up their hospitals, schools and colleges very fast. The weaker provinces did not have even the 50 cents so they were falling further behind.
June 8, 1990

The result was that there was uncontrolled federal spending and the federal government had no idea how much it was going to have to budget each year. So in 1977 the government came out with block funding, the idea that the provinces would just get a certain amount and would then decide how to spend it.
It is true that some provinces have abused that formula. Indeed, there are instances where they have received under the formula more than they have actually spent, for example, on post-secondary education. Nonetheless, it gave more certainty to the federal government and so, on balance, I think that was not so unwise.
The government then moved into a formula that was based on a moving average. The result was that we in Parliament were transferring to the provinces moneys well above the annual rate of inflation. That was not right because we were then giving up the right and

responsibility of parliamentarians to act responsibly in a fiscal sense because, of course, it is the same people being taxed, whether federally or provincially. We have no more right to be irresponsible than do they. Thus, under Bill C-69 with which we just dealt, which is to try to cut back the rate of increase to the provinces, it is still going to be above the rate of inflation, but it will be a lower rate than before.
